Navajo. The Diné, meaning "the People" in their own language, are the largest federally recognized Native American nation, inhabiting the Southwest of Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah. They are known for their distinctive weaving, jewelry, sand painting, and shepherding economy, and they developed a unique cultural synthesis as descendants of Athabaskan migrants.

The Navajo call themselves the Diné, while the Navajo name derives from Spanish sources. Their language is an Athabaskan language distantly related to Apache. They developed a pastoral economy based on sheep herding, which Spanish colonizers had introduced, becoming master weavers whose blankets and rugs are world-renowned. They also created intricate sand paintings as part of healing ceremonies and mastered silverwork and turquoise jewelry-making as trade commodities.

The Navajo were forcibly relocated in the Long Walk from 1864 to 1868, imprisoned at Bosque Redondo, an internment camp where disease and starvation killed thousands. They were freed under the Treaty of 1868. During World War II, approximately four hundred Navajo Code Talkers served in the Marine Corps, using the Diné language as an unbreakable military cipher.

Today the Navajo Nation is the second-largest reservation by population. The Navajo language is actively spoken and taught, with strong sovereignty and cultural revitalization. They remain connected to the Apache, with whom they share Athabaskan heritage and Spanish colonial conflict, and to the memory of the Long Walk, their traumatic forced removal and internment.
